newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkish bankers believe rates have bottomed-out.
newsitem.headline: Turkish bankers believe rates have bottomed-out.

text.p: After a five-week decline in Treasury bill and bond yields, Turkish bankers and brokers now believe interest rates have bottomed-out and may begin to rise.
"The market has begun to say that these levels are the bottom. But at this moment it is important to know what big banks think," said Alp Tekince, assistant general manager of Bumerang securities.
A leading private bank treasurer said she shared the market's expectations. "But a sharp increase is not likely soon," she said.
The Treasury sold 39 trillion lira of 273-day bills to yield 118.75 percent at an auction on Tuesday, down about four points from the previous auction.

Bankers say the Treasury made a mistake when it met only 15 percent of the total demand from banks at Tuesday's auction and left the remaining cash in the market. The excess cash boosted dollar demand and pushed up bond rates by up to four points on Wednesday.
The central bank sold dollars for Turkish lira on Wednesday after the lira fell to below 98,000 against the dollar from Tuesday's close of 97,340.

"Real interest rates, which have fallen to some eight to 10 percent, are now no longer attractive for us to lend to the Treasury for nine months or one year," said Tayyar Ozerdem, general manager of Nurol Securities.

Dealers say the central bank must lower its overnight interest rates or expectations for declining inflation must strengthen before interest rates can decline further. However, there is little expectation of a near-term decline in inflation.
Economists and bankers say any cut in central bank overnight rates might harm the economy and break the fragile stability in financial markets.
A private bank general manager said the central bank had to keep overnight rates stable to achieve its primary aim -- to maintain lira stability and curb inflation.
"Central bank overnight rates should be kept at its present level of 75 percent. Overnight funds may switch to foreign currencies if the central bank lowers overnight quotations," Ozerdem said.
Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan's Islamist Welfare Party has reportedly been urging the Treasury to halt T-bill auctions and lower interest rates.
However, State Minister Ufuk Soylemez said the Treasury would continue auctions in line with its cash needs.
"The balance attained in the lira and foreign currency markets through coordination between the central bank and the Treasury will continue under free market conditions," he told Reuters.
Soylemez said the central bank had high foreign currency reserves of around $17 billion, which he says is enough to weather any speculative attack on the lira.
But economists say foreign currency reserves might be eroded quickly if the lira comes under a strong attack.
